title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ δράκων
part: The Fox and the Snake (Chambry 33 · Perry 268)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 33 (= Perry 268). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation ([ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: [There was a fig tree beside the road.]
sentences.n: Square brackets are Chambry's mark for words he judges to have crept into the text later and would delete — the opposite of the angle brackets he uses for his own additions. Here a whole opening sentence is bracketed: the fig tree plays no part whatever in the story that follows, and looks like the stray first line of some other fable. It is kept here as printed, brackets and all.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ [δὲ] θεασαμένη δράκοντα κοιμώμενον ἐζήλωσεν αὐτοῦ τὸ μῆκος· βουλομένη δὲ αὐτῷ ἐξισωθῆναι παραναπεσοῦσα ἐπειρᾶτο ἑαυτὴν ἐκτείνειν, μέχρις οὗ ὑπερβιαζομένη ἔλαθε ῥαγεῖσα.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx [de] theasamenē drakonta koimōmenon ezēlōsen autou to mēkos· boulomenē de autōi exisōthēnai paranapesousa epeirato heautēn ekteinein, mechris hou hyperbiazomenē elathe rhageisa.
sentences.l: A fox, having beheld a snake sleeping, envied it its length; and wishing to be made equal to it, having lain down beside it, she kept trying to stretch herself out, until, forcing herself too far, she escaped her own notice bursting.
sentences.i: A fox saw a snake asleep and envied it its length; wanting to match it, she lay down alongside and tried to stretch herself out, until she strained too hard and burst before she knew it.
sentences.n: δράκων is a serpent, not the medieval dragon — a large snake, and here simply a long one. ζηλόω here has a single accusative object, τὸ μῆκος, with αὐτοῦ as a possessive genitive: 'envied his length'. (The verb can also take an accusative of the person envied with a genitive of the thing.) ἔλαθε ῥαγεῖσα is λανθάνω with a participle again: 'she burst without noticing it happening'. δέ is bracketed along with the sentence before it: a connective looking back to a clause Chambry deletes has nothing left to join.

sentences.t: Τοῦτο πάσχουσιν οἱ τοῖς κρείττοσιν ἀνθαμιλλώμενοι· θᾶττον γὰρ αὐτοὶ διαρρήγνυνται ἢ ἐκείνων ἐφικέσθαι δύνανται.
sentences.tr: Touto paschousin hoi tois kreittosin anthamillōmenoi· thatton gar autoi diarrēgnyntai ē ekeinōn ephikesthai dynantai.
sentences.l: This is what those suffer who contend against their betters: for they themselves burst asunder sooner than they can reach those others.
sentences.n: A moral with no formula at the front — no 'the story shows', simply Τοῦτο πάσχουσιν οἱ…, 'this is what they suffer who…'. ἀνθαμιλλάομαι, 'match oneself against', takes the dative; ἐφικέσθαι, 'reach, attain to', takes the genitive (ἐκείνων). θᾶττον is the Attic comparative of ταχέως, 'more quickly', answered by ἤ, 'than'.
